screens.title: What makes disaster recovery different from high availability
screens.narratorSegment: Disaster recovery prepares for large-scale, catastrophic events that may affect an entire AWS Region, while high availability and fault tolerance are about reducing localized failures. Define disaster recovery as the set of practices, architectures, and runbooks that restore service after a region-level outage; it often requires cross-region data movement and different operational steps than a single-region failure. A concrete example: Auto scaling plus multiple AZs gives high availability if an instance or an AZ fails, but if the entire Region goes down you need a cross-region plan such as restoring backups or promoting replicas in a secondary Region. A common misconception is to equate multi-AZ redundancy with full disaster recovery. That confusion can leave teams unprepared for regional outages because AZ redundancy doesn't protect against region-wide networking or control-plane failures. Key elements of a DR plan are measurable RTO and RPO, documented recovery steps, and validation tests. As you design a DR strategy, ask: what do stakeholders accept as the maximum downtime and data loss, and does the architecture and runbook meet that expectation? This question will guide whether you choose backups, pilot light, warm standby, or active-active designs.

keyIdea.title: DR vs HA
keyIdea.text: High availability reduces localized downtime; DR prepares services and data for region-level recovery using cross-region strategies and documented runbooks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › DR vs HA
Definition

Disaster recovery

DR prepares for region-level failures using cross-region backups, replicas, and documented recovery steps. It focuses on restoring service under catastrophic conditions, not just single-server faults.

Concrete example

An Auto Scaling group in multiple AZs survives AZ failure but still needs a cross-region plan if the entire Region fails. Backups or a replica in another Region are required for full recovery.

Common misconception

Assuming AZ redundancy equals disaster recovery. AZ redundancy won't help if the Region's control plane or connectivity is impacted.

How to think about it
  • RTO: Maximum acceptable recovery time after a disaster.
  • RPO: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
  • Choose the least complex strategy that satisfies both targets and your budget.
Key Takeaway

Disaster recovery is about region-level resilience: align RTO and RPO with a strategy and test it regularly.

screens.title: Backup & Restore — the low-cost baseline
screens.narratorSegment: Backup and restore is the simplest and most cost-effective disaster recovery strategy. You regularly back up data — AMIs for EC2, snapshots for RDS, and S3 copies — and store them in a separate Region. If a disaster occurs, you restore data and provision new infrastructure in the recovery Region. For example, an internal analytics platform that runs daily reports and can tolerate hours of downtime is a good candidate for backup and restore. The main trade-offs are high RTO and RPO: restoration and provisioning can take hours or days, and data loss is limited to the window between backups. A common mistake is assuming backups alone are sufficient without automation; manual restoration extends RTO and risks configuration drift. To mitigate that, keep infrastructure-as-code templates, pre-built AMIs, and an automated restore script in the recovery Region so provisioning is predictable. The takeaway is that Backup & Restore is right when cost is the priority and the business can accept longer recovery windows; always add automation and verification steps to reduce surprises during a real recovery. Backup & Restore — the low-cost baseline means lowest cost option, highest rto/rpo. good for non-critical workloads when recovery time measured in hours or days is acceptable.. In practical terms, how it works, when to pick it, and its trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Lowest cost option, highest RTO/RPO. Good for non-critical workloads when recovery time measured in hours or days is acceptable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Backup & Restore
Definition

Backup & Restore

Regularly back up data and store backups in another Region. Restore data and provision infrastructure only after a disaster.

When to use
Non-critical workloads that can accept hours or days of downtime and some data loss.
Automation tips
  • - Keep infrastructure-as-code templates in the DR Region.
  • - Pre-build AMIs and scripts to speed provisioning.
  • - Test restores on a schedule to validate backups.
Trade-offs
  • RTO: Hours to days.
  • RPO: Hours, depending on backup frequency.
  • Cost: Low ongoing cost, primarily storage.
Key Takeaway

Backup & Restore is economical for non-critical systems, but automation and repeated restore testing are necessary to make it reliable.

screens.title: Pilot Light — keep the core running
screens.narratorSegment: Pilot Light is like keeping a small, essential core of the system running in the recovery Region so you can scale it up when needed. The core typically includes critical databases or read replicas and a minimal compute footprint that holds configuration and application code updated by your CI/CD pipeline. A concrete example: maintain a cross-region read replica for RDS or S3 cross-region replication for objects, and keep a single small EC2 instance or tiny Auto Scaling Group with the application code in the DR Region. When a disaster occurs, you promote the replica to primary, scale up compute, and update DNS to route traffic to the recovery Region. Pilot Light reduces RTO and RPO compared with plain backups — RTOs are often tens of minutes to a few hours and RPOs are minutes because data is continuously replicated. A common misconception is that pilot light requires no runbook; in reality, promotion steps, DNS updates, and scaling procedures must be automated or well-documented to avoid delays. Choose pilot light when you need faster recovery than backups but want to limit continuous costs.

keyIdea.title: Pilot Light
keyIdea.text: Maintain a minimal, up-to-date core in the DR Region to reduce recovery time and limit continuous cost compared to a warm standby.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Pilot Light
Concept

Pilot Light

Keep a minimal, ready-to-scale core in the DR Region: critical data replicated and small compute running with the application code present.

Typical components
Read replicas for databases, S3 replication for objects, and a small compute footprint with deployment artifacts kept current.
Recovery process
  1. Promote the DB replica to primary and verify data integrity.
  2. Scale compute to production capacity using ASG or templates.
  3. Update DNS so clients route to the DR Region and run smoke tests.
Key Takeaway

Pilot Light balances reduced RTO/RPO with moderate ongoing cost. Automate promotion and DNS changes to achieve predictable recovery times.

screens.title: Warm Standby — run a scaled-down copy continuously
screens.narratorSegment: Warm Standby means running a complete, but scaled-down, version of your production environment in the recovery Region at all times. Essential services are already running and data is continuously replicated, so recovery is usually a matter of scaling resources up and redirecting traffic. For example, you might run smaller EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group behind an ALB in the DR Region, with an RDS replica receiving continuous replication. When a disaster occurs, you increase instance sizes or desired counts and switch DNS. Warm Standby typically achieves RTOs measured in minutes and RPOs in seconds to minutes because replication is continuous. The trade-off is higher ongoing cost compared to Pilot Light due to running many services continuously. A misconception is that warm standby removes the need to practice failover; even when services are running, teams must verify scaling plans, data consistency, and automated DNS failover under load. Warm Standby is appropriate when minimal downtime is required but full multi-region active-active economics are not justified. Warm Standby — run a scaled-down copy continuously means a continuously running, scaled-down duplicate environment that can be scaled to production quickly, offering low rto and low rpo at moderate cost.. In practical terms, a fully provisioned, smaller environment ready to scale to production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Warm Standby
Architecture

Warm Standby

A fully provisioned, smaller-capacity environment runs continuously in the DR Region with data replication in place so it can be scaled to full capacity when needed.

Components
Smaller EC2 fleets or smaller instance sizes, ALBs, continuous DB replication, and synchronized static assets.
When to choose
  • Business-critical applications that tolerate only minutes of downtime.
  • When you need fast scale-up without full active-active cost.
Key Takeaway

Warm Standby offers fast recovery with continuous costs. Always include scale-up validation and failover drills in your test plan.

screens.title: Multi-Site Active/Active — near-zero disruption
screens.narratorSegment: Multi-Site Active/Active deploys your application fully in multiple Regions so each site actively serves traffic. This approach gives the lowest possible RTO and RPO because users are routed to healthy Regions immediately and data synchronization is handled continuously. Examples of technologies used include global DNS routing with latency-based policies or AWS Global Accelerator, and data patterns such as DynamoDB Global Tables or multi-master database setups. The trade-off is significant cost and architectural complexity, particularly around maintaining data consistency across regions and operational processes for deployment and monitoring. A misconception is that active-active simply means duplicating infrastructure; it requires deliberate design for synchronization, conflict resolution, and global traffic routing. Use active-active only for mission-critical systems that cannot tolerate minutes of downtime or data loss. The final design must include observability, automated failover detection, and validation steps so that a region failure results in immediate, seamless continuity for users. Multi-Site Active/Active — near-zero disruption means active-active across regions offers near-zero downtime and data loss but requires complex data synchronization and higher ongoing cost.. In practical terms, fully active deployments across regions and the complexity they bring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Multi-Site Active/Active
Pattern

Active / Active

Fully deploy and serve traffic in multiple Regions with continuous data synchronization and global routing, achieving near-zero RTO and RPO.

Considerations:
  • Data consistency strategies and conflict resolution.
  • Global routing and health checks.
  • Significant operational and cost overhead.
When to pick

Mission-critical systems that require immediate continuity and minimal data loss, such as high-volume financial processing.

Key Takeaway

Active-active provides the best user experience during region failures but adds the highest cost and complexity. Use it only when near-zero RTO and RPO are required.

screens.title: Comparing RTO, RPO, and cost across strategies
screens.narratorSegment: When you compare DR strategies, use a simple matrix: RTO on one axis, RPO on the other, and cost as the third dimension. Backup & Restore sits at the high-RTO, high-RPO, low-cost corner. Pilot Light moves toward lower RTO and RPO with moderate cost by keeping core data and limited compute ready. Warm Standby lowers RTO further by running a full but scaled-down environment continuously. Multi-Site Active/Active gives near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost. A concrete scenario helps: if an internal report generator can tolerate a 12-hour recovery time and one day of data loss, backup & restore is appropriate. If the business requires recovery in minutes with very low data loss, an active-active or warm standby approach is appropriate. Avoid a common error: selecting the highest resilience strategy for every app; this quickly multiplies cost. Instead, group applications by criticality and apply a cost-effective strategy per group. The last practical step is to document the chosen strategy, required AWS services, and the testing cadence so expectations are clear. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › RTO / RPO / Cost
Matrix

RTO, RPO, and Cost

Use a three-factor comparison to assign a strategy: how long can the business tolerate downtime, how much data loss is acceptable, and how much ongoing cost can you budget?

Quick guide
Backup & Restore: high RTO/RPO, low cost. Pilot Light: moderate RTO/RPO, moderate cost. Warm Standby: low RTO/RPO, higher cost. Active/Active: near-zero RTO/RPO, very high cost.
Decision flow
  1. Obtain RTO and RPO targets from stakeholders.
  2. Map targets to the strategy matrix to shortlist approaches.
  3. Estimate cost and pick the least expensive that meets targets.
Key Takeaway

Always align technical choices to measurable business targets and avoid over-engineering every application for the highest resilience level.

screens.title: Replication patterns and AWS services for DR
screens.narratorSegment: Data replication is central to lowering RPO and enabling faster recovery. AWS offers several replication patterns: S3 Cross-Region Replication for static assets, RDS cross-region read replicas for many relational workloads, and DynamoDB Global Tables for globally replicated NoSQL data. Choose S3 replication when static objects must be available in another Region, and remember to replicate bucket configuration and lifecycle rules. Use RDS read replicas when you can promote a replica to primary during recovery; replicas reduce RPO because they continuously receive changes, but promoting requires a coordinated promotion and validation step. Services

S3 · RDS · DynamoDB

S3 Cross-Region Replication

Replicate static assets to another Region for low RPO of object data and fast availability on failover.

RDS read replicas

Replicate relational data and promote a replica to primary during recovery to reduce RPO. Promotion requires orchestration and validation.

screens.title: DNS and traffic failover mechanics
screens.narratorSegment: DNS and traffic routing are critical to restoring service quickly. AWS Route 53 provides routing policies such as failover, latency-based routing, or geolocation routing to move traffic between Regions. In many DR plans you will update DNS records or switch a health-checked failover alias to the secondary Region. For faster, global failover, AWS Global Accelerator can reroute traffic at the network edge. A concrete action during recovery is to ensure TTLs are low enough to reduce propagation time, but not so low that DNS queries cause unnecessary operational cost; plan and agree this TTL with stakeholders. Automate DNS changes as part of your runbook so manual steps do not extend RTO. A common misconception is that simply changing DNS instantly redirects all users; DNS propagation and client caching can still cause delays. Include health checks and smoke tests after traffic is redirected to confirm that the recovery Region is serving requests correctly. Finally, secure DNS changes in your plan and ensure recovery credentials and IAM roles are available in the DR Region. screens.title: Plan, test, and validate your DR runbook
screens.narratorSegment: A well-defined DR plan documents recovery steps, responsible roles, automation, and validation checks. It should list the exact steps to restore each tier, including how to promote replicas, provision infrastructure, update DNS, and verify data integrity. A common mistake is to run only tabletop exercises; you must perform hands-on restores to validate the real operational work. After every test, update the runbook with lessons learned, and keep a testing schedule so the team remains practiced. screens.title: Activity: Choose a DR strategy for a three-tier app

Three-tier web application

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical spectrum of disaster recovery strategies available on AWS and how to choose the one that fits your application and business needs. We will define the four common approaches — Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active/Active — and consistently compare them by Recovery Time Objective, Recovery Point Objective, and ongoing cost. You will see concrete examples that make the differences clear, such as when a daily internal analytics job can tolerate hours of recovery versus a financial system that can tolerate none. I will also point out common mistakes, like over-engineering inexpensive services into multi-region complexity when a simple backup and restore would meet requirements. Finally, you will be introduced to the core AWS patterns used for each approach, including cross-region replication for S3, read replicas for RDS, and DNS failover patterns. By the end you should be able to match a three-tier application’s RTO/RPO needs to a cost-effective DR strategy and know why regular testing and credential management are essential. Which trade-off matters most for your applications?

These learning objectives map to skills you will use when designing or reviewing a disaster recovery plan. First, you will evaluate the four DR strategies — Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active/Active — and learn the concrete trade-offs between cost, recovery time, and data loss tolerance. Second, you will analyze the interplay between RTO and RPO and how business criticality drives those targets. Third, you will identify which strategy fits different application criticality levels and map AWS services such as S3 Cross-Region Replication, RDS read replicas, or DynamoDB global tables to those choices. Finally, you will understand why a written, regularly tested DR plan is essential for reliable recovery and how to include validation steps and credential handling. Each objective includes an example or mnemonic to help you make a defensible recommendation to stakeholders.

On this page we continue the objectives by focusing on practical assessment and communication skills. You will learn how to classify applications by criticality and then choose a DR approach that meets stakeholder expectations at the lowest reasonable cost. We'll practice forming justification statements like, 'Pilot Light meets a four-hour RTO and one-hour RPO at a moderate cost,' versus 'Warm Standby reduces RTO to minutes at higher continuous cost.' You will also learn to document cross-region replication, promote replicas, and include smoke tests in your runbook. A common misconception is that running multiple regions always prevents loss; but without proper replication and promotion steps, multi-region deployment alone may not guarantee fast recovery. Practicing these objectives will make your recommendations clear, measurable, and testable. Learning Objectives — continued means translate technical architecture into plain justifications for stakeholders and provide measurable recovery commitments.. In practical terms, skills for design reviews and stakeholder communication. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Disaster recovery prepares for large-scale, catastrophic events that may affect an entire AWS Region, while high availability and fault tolerance are about reducing localized failures. Define disaster recovery as the set of practices, architectures, and runbooks that restore service after a region-level outage; it often requires cross-region data movement and different operational steps than a single-region failure. A concrete example: Auto scaling plus multiple AZs gives high availability if an instance or an AZ fails, but if the entire Region goes down you need a cross-region plan such as restoring backups or promoting replicas in a secondary Region. A common misconception is to equate multi-AZ redundancy with full disaster recovery. That confusion can leave teams unprepared for regional outages because AZ redundancy doesn't protect against region-wide networking or control-plane failures. Key elements of a DR plan are measurable RTO and RPO, documented recovery steps, and validation tests. As you design a DR strategy, ask: what do stakeholders accept as the maximum downtime and data loss, and does the architecture and runbook meet that expectation? This question will guide whether you choose backups, pilot light, warm standby, or active-active designs.

Backup and restore is the simplest and most cost-effective disaster recovery strategy. You regularly back up data — AMIs for EC2, snapshots for RDS, and S3 copies — and store them in a separate Region. If a disaster occurs, you restore data and provision new infrastructure in the recovery Region. For example, an internal analytics platform that runs daily reports and can tolerate hours of downtime is a good candidate for backup and restore. The main trade-offs are high RTO and RPO: restoration and provisioning can take hours or days, and data loss is limited to the window between backups. A common mistake is assuming backups alone are sufficient without automation; manual restoration extends RTO and risks configuration drift. To mitigate that, keep infrastructure-as-code templates, pre-built AMIs, and an automated restore script in the recovery Region so provisioning is predictable. The takeaway is that Backup & Restore is right when cost is the priority and the business can accept longer recovery windows; always add automation and verification steps to reduce surprises during a real recovery. Backup & Restore — the low-cost baseline means lowest cost option, highest rto/rpo. good for non-critical workloads when recovery time measured in hours or days is acceptable.. In practical terms, how it works, when to pick it, and its trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pilot Light is like keeping a small, essential core of the system running in the recovery Region so you can scale it up when needed. The core typically includes critical databases or read replicas and a minimal compute footprint that holds configuration and application code updated by your CI/CD pipeline. A concrete example: maintain a cross-region read replica for RDS or S3 cross-region replication for objects, and keep a single small EC2 instance or tiny Auto Scaling Group with the application code in the DR Region. When a disaster occurs, you promote the replica to primary, scale up compute, and update DNS to route traffic to the recovery Region. Pilot Light reduces RTO and RPO compared with plain backups — RTOs are often tens of minutes to a few hours and RPOs are minutes because data is continuously replicated. A common misconception is that pilot light requires no runbook; in reality, promotion steps, DNS updates, and scaling procedures must be automated or well-documented to avoid delays. Choose pilot light when you need faster recovery than backups but want to limit continuous costs.

Warm Standby means running a complete, but scaled-down, version of your production environment in the recovery Region at all times. Essential services are already running and data is continuously replicated, so recovery is usually a matter of scaling resources up and redirecting traffic. For example, you might run smaller EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group behind an ALB in the DR Region, with an RDS replica receiving continuous replication. When a disaster occurs, you increase instance sizes or desired counts and switch DNS. Warm Standby typically achieves RTOs measured in minutes and RPOs in seconds to minutes because replication is continuous. The trade-off is higher ongoing cost compared to Pilot Light due to running many services continuously. A misconception is that warm standby removes the need to practice failover; even when services are running, teams must verify scaling plans, data consistency, and automated DNS failover under load. Warm Standby is appropriate when minimal downtime is required but full multi-region active-active economics are not justified. Warm Standby — run a scaled-down copy continuously means a continuously running, scaled-down duplicate environment that can be scaled to production quickly, offering low rto and low rpo at moderate cost.. In practical terms, a fully provisioned, smaller environment ready to scale to production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Multi-Site Active/Active deploys your application fully in multiple Regions so each site actively serves traffic. This approach gives the lowest possible RTO and RPO because users are routed to healthy Regions immediately and data synchronization is handled continuously. Examples of technologies used include global DNS routing with latency-based policies or AWS Global Accelerator, and data patterns such as DynamoDB Global Tables or multi-master database setups. The trade-off is significant cost and architectural complexity, particularly around maintaining data consistency across regions and operational processes for deployment and monitoring. A misconception is that active-active simply means duplicating infrastructure; it requires deliberate design for synchronization, conflict resolution, and global traffic routing. Use active-active only for mission-critical systems that cannot tolerate minutes of downtime or data loss. The final design must include observability, automated failover detection, and validation steps so that a region failure results in immediate, seamless continuity for users. Multi-Site Active/Active — near-zero disruption means active-active across regions offers near-zero downtime and data loss but requires complex data synchronization and higher ongoing cost.. In practical terms, fully active deployments across regions and the complexity they bring. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you compare DR strategies, use a simple matrix: RTO on one axis, RPO on the other, and cost as the third dimension. Backup & Restore sits at the high-RTO, high-RPO, low-cost corner. Pilot Light moves toward lower RTO and RPO with moderate cost by keeping core data and limited compute ready. Warm Standby lowers RTO further by running a full but scaled-down environment continuously. Multi-Site Active/Active gives near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost. A concrete scenario helps: if an internal report generator can tolerate a 12-hour recovery time and one day of data loss, backup & restore is appropriate. If the business requires recovery in minutes with very low data loss, an active-active or warm standby approach is appropriate. Avoid a common error: selecting the highest resilience strategy for every app; this quickly multiplies cost. Instead, group applications by criticality and apply a cost-effective strategy per group. The last practical step is to document the chosen strategy, required AWS services, and the testing cadence so expectations are clear. Comparing RTO, RPO, and cost across strategies means place each application on a matrix of rto vs rpo and choose the least-costly strategy that meets those constraints.. In practical terms, a concise matrix to guide selection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Data replication is central to lowering RPO and enabling faster recovery. AWS offers several replication patterns: S3 Cross-Region Replication for static assets, RDS cross-region read replicas for many relational workloads, and DynamoDB Global Tables for globally replicated NoSQL data. Choose S3 replication when static objects must be available in another Region, and remember to replicate bucket configuration and lifecycle rules. Use RDS read replicas when you can promote a replica to primary during recovery; replicas reduce RPO because they continuously receive changes, but promoting requires a coordinated promotion and validation step. For multi-master or globally active needs, DynamoDB global tables provide active-active replication at the data layer, reducing RTO/RPO but demanding design attention for consistency. A common pitfall is assuming replication alone is sufficient; you must also provision permissions, parameter groups, and automation to promote replicas and validate integrity after promotion.
